chapter.name: Patterns in Mathematics
chapter.blurb: Number sequences and shape sequences, how to recognise and extend them, and the surprising additive relations that connect different sequences to each other.

scope_in.item: Recognise and extend the basic number sequences: All 1's, counting numbers, odd numbers, even numbers, triangular numbers, square numbers, cube numbers, Virahanka numbers, powers of 2 and powers of 3

Represent number sequences pictorially with dot arrangements -- squares as square grids, triangular numbers as staircases, cubes as three-dimensional dot blocks -- and explain the sequence names from the pictures
Explain, using a dot picture, why the sum of consecutive odd numbers starting from 1 always gives a perfect square, and compute such sums, e.g. the sum of the first 10 or first 100 odd numbers
Explain, using a dot picture, why adding the counting numbers 'up and down' (1+2+...+n+...+2+1) gives a perfect square

Identify and use further additive relations among number sequences: consecutive triangular numbers sum to a square number; 6 times a triangular number plus 1 gives a hexagonal number; the running sum of powers of 2 starting at 1, plus 1, gives the next power of 2; the running sum of hexagonal numbers gives cube numbers
Recognise and extend the basic shape sequences: regular polygons, complete graphs, stacked triangles, stacked squares, and Koch Snowflake iterations

Relate a counted feature of a shape sequence to a number sequence already met: number of sides/corners of regular polygons to counting numbers from 3; number of lines in complete graphs to triangular numbers; number of small squares/triangles in the stacked sequences to square numbers; number of segments in the Koch Snowflake to 3 times powers of 4

scope_out.item: Formal algebraic notation for the nth term of a sequence (e.g. a subscript n equals n squared) or summation notation
scope_out.reason: This chapter's explanations are entirely pictorial and inductive; variables and algebraic notation are not introduced until later chapters

scope_out.item: Arithmetic and geometric progression formulas for the nth term or sum of a progression
scope_out.reason: Not this book's method here; results are justified by pictures and pattern-spotting, not by formula derivation
Covered separately in Chapter 5, Prime Time

scope_out.item: Angles and properties of lines, including angle sums of polygons
scope_out.reason: Covered separately in Chapter 2, Lines and Angles

scope_out.item: Perimeter and area formulas of squares or other shapes
scope_out.reason: Covered separately in Chapter 6, Perimeter and Area; the square-dot pictures here are only for counting, not for measuring physical area

scope_out.item: Symmetry of the shape sequences shown, e.g. rotational symmetry of the Koch Snowflake
The golden ratio or any connection between Virahanka numbers and the golden ratio
scope_out.reason: Not mentioned anywhere in this chapter; would be pulling in an outside fact the book does not use here

concepts.name: Number sequences
concepts.description: The basic number sequences studied in this chapter -- counting numbers, odd numbers, even numbers, triangular numbers, squares, cubes, Virahanka numbers, powers of 2 and powers of 3 -- and the rule that generates each one.
concepts.idea: A number sequence is a list of numbers that follows a rule; once you spot the rule you can predict any later term without listing every number in between.
concepts.rule: Counting numbers add 1 each time; odd/even numbers add 2 each time; triangular numbers add the next counting number; squares are n multiplied by itself; cubes are n multiplied by itself three times; Virahanka numbers add the two terms before; powers of 2 double each time; powers of 3 triple each time.
concepts.example: The triangular numbers 1, 3, 6, 10, 15, ... continue 21, 28, 36 because each new term adds one more than the last addition (add 6, then 7, then 8).

questions.q: Explain why the sequence of Virahanka numbers 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 21, ... cannot be produced by 'multiply the previous term by a fixed number', unlike the powers of 2 or powers of 3 sequences. Support your answer with two consecutive ratios from the sequence.
questions.a: In powers of 2 or 3 every term is the previous term times a fixed number (2 or 3), but in the Virahanka sequence the ratio between consecutive terms keeps changing, e.g. 3/2 = 1.5 and 8/5 = 1.6, so no single fixed multiplier works; instead each term is the sum of the two before it.

concepts.name: Visualising number sequences with pictures
concepts.description: Representing number sequences as dot pictures -- squares as square grids, triangular numbers as staircases, cubes as three-dimensional blocks -- to see why each sequence is named as it is.
concepts.idea: Drawing the numbers of a sequence as a picture of dots can show directly why the sequence has the name it does, and can reveal that the same number sometimes fits more than one picture.
concepts.rule: A square number n squared is a grid of n rows and n dots per row; a triangular number is a staircase with 1, 2, 3, ..., n dots in successive rows; a cube number n cubed is a block n dots long, n wide and n high.
concepts.example: 36 dots form a perfect 6-by-6 square, and also a triangular staircase of 8 rows (1+2+...+8=36), so 36 is both a square number and a triangular number.

concepts.name: Sum of consecutive odd numbers gives square numbers
concepts.description: The result that adding up the first few odd numbers, starting from 1, always gives a perfect square, shown with a dot picture and used to compute sums quickly.
concepts.idea: There is a hidden connection between two different-looking sequences: odd numbers and squares -- adding enough odd numbers in a row always lands exactly on a square number.
concepts.rule: The sum of the first n odd numbers, starting at 1, equals n squared: 1 + 3 + 5 + ... + (2n-1) = n squared.
concepts.example: The sum of the first 6 odd numbers, 1+3+5+7+9+11, equals 36, which is 6 squared.

concepts.name: Other relations among number sequences
concepts.description: Further additive relationships connecting the number sequences of this chapter: consecutive triangular numbers summing to squares, six times a triangular number plus one giving a hexagonal number, and running sums of powers of 2 and of hexagonal numbers producing the next power of 2 and cube numbers respectively.
concepts.idea: Number sequences that look unrelated are often linked by a simple addition rule; finding the rule lets you jump between sequences.
concepts.rule: Two consecutive triangular numbers add to a square number; 6 times a triangular number, plus 1, gives a hexagonal number; the running sum of powers of 2 starting at 1, plus 1, gives the next power of 2; the running sum of hexagonal numbers gives cube numbers.

concepts.name: Shape sequences
concepts.description: The basic shape sequences of this chapter -- regular polygons, complete graphs, stacked triangles, stacked squares and the Koch Snowflake -- and the rule that builds each next shape.
concepts.idea: Just as numbers form sequences, shapes can too; each shape sequence follows its own rule for turning one shape into the next.
concepts.rule: Regular polygons gain one side each step, starting from the triangle; a complete graph K(n) joins every one of its n dots to every other dot; the Koch Snowflake replaces every straight segment with a bent 'speed bump' at each step.
concepts.example: The regular-polygon sequence goes triangle, quadrilateral, pentagon, hexagon, ... -- one more side each time.

Complete graphs: from the 3rd term (K4, 6 lines) to the 6th term (K7, 21 lines), lines go from 6 to 21, an increase of 15. questions.q: A classmate says 'the Koch Snowflake sequence and the regular-polygon sequence both just get more sides, so they're basically the same kind of pattern'. Do you agree? Justify briefly.
questions.a: Disagree -- regular polygons add exactly one more straight side each step (3, 4, 5, 6, ...), while the Koch Snowflake replaces every existing segment with a bent shape, so its segment count multiplies by 4 each step (3, 12, 48, 192, ...); the two patterns grow in fundamentally different ways.

concepts.name: Relating shape sequences to number sequences
concepts.description: Counting a feature of a shape sequence -- its sides, corners, small tiles or line segments -- and recognising that the resulting count matches a number sequence already studied.
concepts.idea: A shape sequence and a number sequence can be two different views of the very same pattern; counting the right feature of the shapes reveals the matching number sequence.
concepts.rule: Regular polygons: sides = corners = counting numbers from 3. Complete graphs: number of connecting lines = triangular numbers. Stacked squares/triangles: number of small pieces = square numbers. Koch Snowflake: number of line segments = 3 times powers of 4.
concepts.example: The complete graph K5 has 10 connecting lines, which is the 4th triangular number.

questions.a: The claim is false. The 4th regular polygon (hexagon) has 6 sides. The 4th complete-graph term, K5, has 10 lines. Since 6 does not equal 10, the two sequences are different, disproving the claim.
